summary: NTP version 4 lets packets carry optional extension fields after the standard header, for capabilities the basic header cannot convey. This standards-track RFC clarifies several points about how those fields are formatted and how they interact with Message Authentication Codes (MACs). It updates RFC 5905, the core NTPv4 specification.

eli5.summary: Clocks sending time messages sometimes want to attach extra notes. This sets clearer rules for where the notes go and how to sign the message so nobody can sneak changes in.

questions: how do ntp extension fields work with mac
can an ntp packet have extension fields without a mac
how long can an ntp extension field be
what happens with unknown ntp extension fields
subtitle: Clarifies where optional NTP extension fields go, how they pair with a MAC, and what hosts do with fields they do not know.

tldr.problem: NTPv4 allows optional extension fields and optional Message Authentication Codes (MACs), but RFC 5905 left their relationship unclear and even said a MAC is always present when an extension field is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7822 rewrites Section 7.5 of RFC 5905: extension fields come before a MAC only if one is present, unknown field types are ignored, and a new set of length and algorithm rules covers every combination of fields and MACs.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get precise rules for parsing packets with extension fields. RFC 7822 itself is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 9748.

facts.label: Minimum without a MAC
facts.value: 28 octets for the last (or only) field

facts.label: Padding
facts.value: Zero-padded to a four-octet word boundary

today: RFC 7822 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5905 and is itself updated by RFC 9748. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Extension Fields Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
An NTP packet has a fixed header that can be followed by two kinds of optional field: a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and extension fields. A MAC sits at the end of the packet and is either 24 octets, 20 octets, or a 4-octet crypto-NAK. Extension fields were defined in RFC 5905 as a generic way to add future features without changing the NTP header.

When this RFC was written, the only extension fields in use were those of the Autokey protocol and the Checksum Complement from RFC 7821. Autokey fields are always followed by a MAC, but a MAC is not mandatory after an extension field. RFC 5905 and an erratum already said so; this document makes the point explicit.

RFC 7822 updates Section 7.5 of RFC 5905. It clarifies how extension fields relate to MACs and defines what a host does when it receives an unknown extension field.
sections.eli5: A time message can have extra notes and a signature. People were unsure whether a note always needs a signature. This paper says no, and sorts out the rest.

sections.title: The Extension Field Format
sections.content:
An extension field has a Field Type and a Length, then a Value and Padding. All extension fields are zero-padded to a word (four octets) boundary. The Length field is a 16-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the whole extension field in octets, padding included.

The old text said one or more extension fields come after the header and before the MAC, which is always present. The new text says they come before the MAC if a MAC is present.

The minimum field length is four words (16 octets). The RFC adds an upper bound: because of the size of the Length field, a field cannot be longer than 65532 octets.
sections.eli5: Each note has a label, a size, the message itself and some blank space so it ends neatly. The size says how big the whole note is, blanks included.

sections.title: Unknown Field Types
sections.content:
The Field Type value is defined in an IANA registry. The Length, Value and Padding are defined by the document that the registry points to.

The new rule for unknown types is simple. A host that receives an extension field with an unknown Field Type SHOULD ignore that field. It MAY drop the whole packet if its policy requires it.

Ignoring unknown fields is what lets new extension fields be added later without breaking hosts that do not understand them yet.
sections.eli5: If you get a note in a language you cannot read, you just skip it. If your rules are strict, you may throw away the whole letter.

sections.title: Extension Fields and MACs
sections.content:
A specification that defines a new extension field MUST say whether the field requires a MAC. If it does, the specification MUST define the algorithm used to create the MAC and the length of the MAC. A field MAY allow more than one algorithm, but then the field itself MUST say which algorithm was used.

When several extension fields in one packet require a MAC, they MUST all require the same algorithm and MAC length. Fields that do not need a MAC can be mixed in with those that do. A packet MUST NOT be sent with two or more MAC-requiring fields that use different algorithms. A receiver that gets such a packet, with fields it recognizes, MUST discard it.

Without any extension field, a MAC MUST NOT be longer than 24 octets unless client and server agree on a longer one. They can agree through an earlier exchange of packets with an extension field that defines the MAC size and algorithm.
sections.eli5: If several notes each need a signature, they must all use the same kind of signature. Mixing two kinds in one letter is not allowed, and the receiver throws such a letter away.

sections.title: Length Rules Without a MAC
sections.content:
If no MAC is present, one or more extension fields can follow the header under two length rules, which let a receiver tell an extension field from a MAC.

  • A packet with a single extension field: its length MUST be at least 7 words, that is, at least 28 octets.
  • A packet with more than one extension field: the last field MUST be at least 28 octets, and each of the others at least 16 octets.
sections.eli5: Notes with no signature must be big enough that nobody mistakes one for a signature. The last note has to be a bit bigger than the others.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that extension fields cannot be used to amplify a Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack on NTP servers. Servers ignore unknown extension fields and answer only with known ones. Extension fields from incoming packets are neither propagated nor included in a response; a server creates its own fields if it needs them.

A server should flag a large number of extension fields as a potential attack, and large field sizes too unless they are expected.

Middleboxes such as firewalls MUST NOT filter NTP packets based on their extension fields. They should not examine the fields at all, since packets may carry new fields the middlebox has not been updated to recognize.
sections.eli5: A time server does not copy notes from incoming letters into its replies, so bad guys cannot use notes to make it shout. Gatekeepers on the road must not block letters just because of the notes inside.

fields.name: Field Type
fields.desc: Identifies the extension; its values are defined in an IANA registry.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the entire extension field in octets, including Padding.
